targets.tagline: Two brown dwarfs orbiting each other every 12 days
targets.about: Xuan et al. (2024) used VLTI/GRAVITY to split the brown dwarf Gl 229 B into a tight pair, Ba and Bb. We fit the same nights of closure phases with a Keplerian orbit and draw it against their two orbits (PMOIRED and Octofitter).

notes.title: Conventions
notes.text: Xuan et al. give ω for the primary (Ba). virgil's ω is the companion's, so ours is the published value + 180°. Their semi-major axis is in au; we convert it to mas with the parallax (173.574 mas). The published curves drawn here already include both conversions.

notes.title: Visibility contrast
notes.text: GRAVITY's V² loses contrast by a different amount each night, so the fit gives each night its own V² amplitude rather than one for the whole run. The flux ratio, read from the same amplitudes, depends on it.

notes.title: Reference-informed fit
notes.text: No published orbit enters the fit, but the 10 to 14 d period window is centred on the published period, so the winning band is a choice among a few bands, not an independent confirmation. Every period band in the window is searched (per-night positions, the two single-night alias peaks flagged, the 2024-12-19 night left out) and the best-evidence band is refitted. This is the maximum-likelihood orbit of the six usable nights of the ESO archive; no posterior sampling yet; the table lists the modes. The five-night OiDB collection alone (125 d) lands in the same band but constrains the elements more loosely.

notes.title: Radial velocities
notes.text: The paper combines the astrometry with radial velocities; ours is astrometry only. Orbital elements are therefore reported, not scored.

targets.tagline: A Be star and a stripped companion on a 40-day orbit
targets.about: Klement et al. (2025) combined VLTI/GRAVITY astrometry of the inner pair of HR 6819 with radial velocities to get dynamical masses. We fit the astrometry alone.

notes.title: Conventions
notes.text: No ω shift is needed. Table 3 of the paper labels its ω as the Be star's, but the number matches the companion's ω in Table 2 (astrometry only), and virgil's ω is the companion's too, so the published ω is used as it stands (settled in virgil-validation PR #102). The circular-orbit curves are drawn for completeness: their T₀ is a time of superior conjunction, and in Table 3 it looks half a period away from Table 2's.

notes.title: Not a clean target
notes.text: A Be star's decretion disk adds light that a model of two point stars does not describe. Every row is compared but never scored, so the badge reads 'reported'.

targets.tagline: A 10-day spectroscopic binary seen by CHARA/MIRC-X
targets.about: Anugu et al. (2020) fitted five nights of CHARA/MIRC-X data on ι Peg (HD 210027) and compared the orbit with the spectroscopic one of Konacki et al. (2010). We fit the same files.

notes.title: Conventions
notes.text: The paper does not say which component its ω refers to, nor whether T_peri is an MJD or an RJD (MJD + 0.5), and its Ω is epoch-of-date rather than J2000. We take ω and T_peri as published, so the drawn curves may be out of phase by up to half a period or a degree-scale rotation: they are a guide, and the elements are reported, not scored.

targets.about: Schaefer et al. (2016) measured the σ Ori Aa-Ab orbit from MIRC data. targets.tagline: An O3.5 V + O5.5 V binary on a 9-year, e = 0.65 orbit, seen by three VLTI instruments
targets.about: Le Bouquin et al. (2017) followed 9 Sgr (HD 164794) with AMBER, PIONIER and GRAVITY and fitted the 18 positions together with radial velocities; Fabry et al. (2021) added five epochs and refitted. The orbit is drawn here for context. Raw frames are being reduced with the instrument pipelines (pndrs, amdlib, the ESO GRAVITY pipeline), and the blind fit has not been run: this is the 'awaiting blind fit' placeholder.

notes.title: Conventions
notes.text: Both papers give ω for the secondary and PA east of north, as virgil does, so no shift is applied (the published orbit reproduces the 18 published positions to 0.19 mas rms; positions cannot check the sign of ω and Ω, which only radial velocities fix, so compare them modulo the joint 180° flip). Fabry et al. do not tabulate a semi-major axis: the 14.83 mas drawn for their orbit is derived from their masses, period and distance.

notes.title: Two published orbits
notes.text: Le Bouquin et al. find P = 3310 d and a mass tension; Fabry et al. find P = 3261 ± 69 d and resolve it. Both are drawn; the first is the headline.

notes.title: Archival data
notes.text: The six earliest PIONIER nights (2012 to mid-2013) have no public raw frames and cannot be reduced; the three GRAVITY nights have the calibrator HD 164031. Details in design/9sgr_onboarding.md.

data.archive: ESO science archive (raw frames, public): VLTI/AMBER, PIONIER and GRAVITY, 17 of the 23 published epochs (16 nights)

targets.about: Le Bouquin et al. (2017) published a preliminary astrometric orbit of HD 168137 from 11 nights of AMBER and PIONIER data. The orbit is badly constrained (a = 7.0 ± 3.9 mas, e = 0.90 ± 0.06) and the periastron falls in a gap, so a broad blind posterior is the expected result, not a failure. Awaiting the blind fit.

notes.title: Preliminary orbit
notes.text: The paper calls its orbit preliminary and ignores the radial velocities. i = 105°, so the orbit runs clockwise on the sky. Elements are reported, not scored.

targets.tagline: A 3.98099-day binary (mostly below the resolution limit)
targets.about: Gallenne et al. 2023 (GRAVITY) measured 12 positions of AK For and fitted an orbit with radial velocities. No orbit has been fitted here yet: a blind solver, with no published starting values, will fit the paper's nights and be scored on the 9 further nights it has not seen. The published orbit is drawn for comparison only.

notes.title: Conventions
notes.text: Elements from Gallenne et al. 2023, Table 6 (joint radial-velocity and astrometry fit). omega is the primary's (the RV model is V1 = gamma + K1[cos(omega + nu) + e cos omega], V2 with -K2); T_peri is a full JD (here also as MJD = JD - 2400000.5). Omega is the position angle of the ascending node, measured east of north, with the equinox not stated; the time scale of T_peri (UTC, HJD or BJD) is not stated. Positions are the secondary relative to the primary (east and north positive). Checked against the paper's own tables: the tabulated omega and Omega, used as they stand in the standard Campbell formulas, reproduce the published positions (Table B.1); changing either alone by 180 degrees does not. (Equivalent to the companion's omega + 180 degrees with Omega + 180 degrees.) Where e is near zero (AK For, o Leo) omega and T_peri are poorly determined. Compare orbits on the sky by their Thiele-Innes constants (orbit.thiele_innes_mas: with X = cos E - e, Y = sqrt(1 - e^2) sin E, dDec = A X + F Y and dRA = B X + G Y): they do not depend on which star omega refers to or on the (omega, Omega) -> (omega + 180, Omega + 180) degeneracy of astrometry without radial velocities. For kappa Vel they are taken from the paper's own Eqs. 6-7.

notes.title: Held-out split
notes.text: 12 nights are the paper's (12 files, plus 1 from the same nights); 9 files on 9 other nights are held out, 0 of them after the paper's last epoch. ESO Phase 3 products, public; the fit never sees the held-out nights.

notes.title: Below the resolution limit
notes.text: 12 of 12 published positions are closer than λ/2B (about 1.75 mas for GRAVITY K at 130 m): the authors' positions come from model fitting below the formal resolution.

notes.title: Caveats
notes.text: Errors include systematic floors (8-50 uas), so the smallest ellipses are floors not statistical errors. Astrometry is SC-only. The paper's orbit used these positions, so orbit predictions at these epochs are consistency checks only. The Phase 3 products are uncalibrated (SINGLE_SCI_VIS): use closure phases only.

notes.title: Conventions
notes.text: Elements from Gallenne et al. 2023, Table 6 (joint radial-velocity and astrometry fit). omega is the primary's (the RV model is V1 = gamma + K1[cos(omega + nu) + e cos omega], V2 with -K2); T_peri is a full JD (here also as MJD = JD - 2400000.5). Omega is the position angle of the ascending node, measured east of north, with the equinox not stated; the time scale of T_peri (UTC, HJD or BJD) is not stated. Positions are the secondary relative to the primary (east and north positive). Checked against the paper's own tables: the tabulated omega and Omega, used as they stand in the standard Campbell formulas, reproduce the published positions (Table B.1); changing either alone by 180 degrees does not. (Equivalent to the companion's omega + 180 degrees with Omega + 180 degrees.) Where e is near zero (AK For, o Leo) omega and T_peri are poorly determined. Compare orbits on the sky by their Thiele-Innes constants (orbit.thiele_innes_mas: with X = cos E - e, Y = sqrt(1 - e^2) sin E, dDec = A X + F Y and dRA = B X + G Y): they do not depend on which star omega refers to or on the (omega, Omega) -> (omega + 180, Omega + 180) degeneracy of astrometry without radial velocities. For kappa Vel they are taken from the paper's own Eqs. 6-7.

notes.title: Caveats

Diagnosis (2026-10-20, from the run's own reports): the period window (3.6-2864 d) contains the published 36.5 d. The per-night position search agrees with the paper's positions on 4 of 10 nights (MJD 59191, 59498, 59819, 59907). On 5 further nights (59523, 59538, 59817, 59877, 59904) the dRA is right but the dDec is off by 3-15 mas (a north-south sidelobe; fitted separations 4.3-13.4 mas against the orbit's maximum of about 5.5 mas), and no night flag fired on them. Raw chi2/N is 22-104 on every night, so the likelihood was tempered by 1/854 and the orbit-versus-single-star evidence is only 2.4 nats. The long-period winner is therefore driven by wrong night positions, not by a missed window.
Short-arc seeding (virgil#425) was not in this run: with few nights far apart the cycle count may be narrower than the band ranking here shows.

notes.title: Conventions
notes.text: Elements from Rowan, Kraus and Thompson 2026, Table 4 (joint SB1 radial-velocity and GRAVITY astrometry fit). omega is the photometric primary's. T0 (73.1 d) is printed without an epoch: JD - 2416500 is the scale of the paper's RV table and the only offset that fits it, so T_peri here is derived, not stated. The paper's Omega and i are in a form (Thiele-Innes constants with x = -A(cosE - e) - F sqrt(1-e^2) sinE) that does not give the published positions in the standard east-of-north Campbell formulas; the equivalent standard elements, found here by comparing the paper's Eqs. 6-7 with the standard form and then tried against Table 3; their Thiele-Innes constants equal those of the paper's own Eqs. 6-7 to 1e-15, so the mapping is exact algebra, not a fit to Table 3), are Omega = 270 - 109.74 = 160.26 degrees and i = 180 - 74.03 = 105.97 degrees (retrograde, as the position angles run). Use 'standard' for any comparison; the published values stay in 'orbit'. Omega is the position angle of the ascending node, measured east of north, with the equinox not stated; the time scale of T_peri (UTC, HJD or BJD) is not stated. Positions are the secondary relative to the primary (east and north positive).  Compare orbits on the sky by their Thiele-Innes constants (orbit.thiele_innes_mas: with X = cos E - e, Y = sqrt(1 - e^2) sin E, dDec = A X + F Y and dRA = B X + G Y): they do not depend on which star omega refers to or on the (omega, Omega) -> (omega + 180, Omega + 180) degeneracy of astrometry without radial velocities. For kappa Vel they are taken from the paper's own Eqs. 6-7.

notes.title: Held-out split
notes.text: 9 nights are the paper's (8 files); there are no other public nights. ESO Phase 3 products, public; the fit never sees the held-out nights.

notes.title: Caveats
notes.text: Single-field AT; sep 2.7-6.6 mas so well inside fibre. Astrometric residuals required scaling bootstrapped errors by s_ast ~ 2.2 (ln s_ast=0.8). Quoted sigma are bootstrap values and underestimate scatter. Separation never below ~2.7 mas vs resolution ~1 mas. Resolution lambda/2D=1.0 mas at 201.5 m. Calibrators differ per night (UD diameters in Table 1). Primary is B2IV photometric primary; the secondary is detected at first epoch.

notes.text: Elements from Gallenne et al. 2023, Table 6 (joint radial-velocity and astrometry fit). omega is the primary's (the RV model is V1 = gamma + K1[cos(omega + nu) + e cos omega], V2 with -K2); T_peri is a full JD (here also as MJD = JD - 2400000.5). Omega is the position angle of the ascending node, measured east of north, with the equinox not stated; the time scale of T_peri (UTC, HJD or BJD) is not stated. Positions are the secondary relative to the primary (east and north positive). Checked against the paper's own tables: the tabulated omega and Omega, used as they stand in the standard Campbell formulas, reproduce the published positions (Table B.1); changing either alone by 180 degrees does not. (Equivalent to the companion's omega + 180 degrees with Omega + 180 degrees.) Where e is near zero (AK For, o Leo) omega and T_peri are poorly determined. Compare orbits on the sky by their Thiele-Innes constants (orbit.thiele_innes_mas: with X = cos E - e, Y = sqrt(1 - e^2) sin E, dDec = A X + F Y and dRA = B X + G Y): they do not depend on which star omega refers to or on the (omega, Omega) -> (omega + 180, Omega + 180) degeneracy of astrometry without radial velocities. For kappa Vel they are taken from the paper's own Eqs. 6-7.

notes.title: Held-out split
notes.text: 8 nights are the paper's (8 files); 18 files on 12 other nights are held out, 2 of them after the paper's last epoch. ESO Phase 3 products, public; the fit never sees the held-out nights.

notes.title: Below the resolution limit
notes.text: 8 of 8 published positions are closer than λ/2B (about 1.75 mas for GRAVITY K at 130 m): the authors' positions come from model fitting below the formal resolution.

notes.title: Caveats
notes.text: Errors include systematic floors (8-50 uas), so the smallest ellipses are floors not statistical errors. Astrometry is SC-only. The paper's orbit used these positions, so orbit predictions at these epochs are consistency checks only. The Phase 3 products are uncalibrated (SINGLE_SCI_VIS): use closure phases only.

guide.title: The sky plane
guide.text: North is up and east is to the left, as on the sky, so ΔRA increases towards the left. The primary star is the gold dot at the origin, both axes are in milliarcseconds (mas), and the scale bar gives the length on the sky.

guide.title: virgil's orbit
guide.text: The solid blue line is our maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) orbit: the single best Keplerian orbit fitted to all the nights at once.

guide.title: Published orbits
guide.text: Dashed lines are the orbits in the paper, converted to virgil's conventions (see each target's notes). Where the paper gives several solutions, the headline one is orange and the others follow in other hues.

guide.title: Alternative modes
guide.text: The faint grey lines are other local optima that the multi-start search found in the likelihood, each refitted to convergence. Δloss is how much higher its loss (the negative log posterior) is than the MAP's: a few units cannot be ruled out, hundreds are clearly worse. They are shown because an orbit fit can lock onto an alias (a different number of cycles between nights) or a mirror image, and the reader should see what else the data allow. Only credible modes are drawn, those within Δloss ≤ 10 nats of the MAP; the page says how many worse ones were hidden, and the axes are set by our orbit, the published orbit and the nights alone.

guide.title: Epoch points
guide.text: Each filled blue dot is the companion's position on one night, from fitting that night alone, with its 1σ error ellipse. Open orange rings are the paper's own position for that night, where it gives one. Hover over a dot, or tab to it, for the date, separation and position angle.

guide.title: Alias nights
guide.text: A cross with a dashed ellipse marks a night that virgil flagged alias-peaks: its best single-night peak is a secondary maximum of the likelihood, not the companion's true position. Such nights are not expected to sit on the orbit. Other flags (separation below the resolution limit, chi2 too high, flux at its bound, low gap) are drawn as open diamonds, not crosses, with the reason in the tooltip; the tooltip and the legend say whether the night was excluded from the orbit fit.

guide.title: Phase panels
guide.text: Separation and position angle against orbital phase, with phase 0 at periastron. Each curve is folded on its own period; the dots are our nights placed on our orbit. A target without an orbit shows the published orbit if there is one, else the positions against date.

items.title: agrees
items.text: At least one comparison was scored and every scored comparison passed.

items.title: tension
items.text: At least one scored comparison failed, or virgil did not deliver a quantity that is scored. Not a verdict on virgil: a convention, the data or the model may be at fault, and the notes say what is known.

items.title: reported
items.text: Nothing is scored. Everything is compared and shown, but not as a pass or fail: orbital elements, because the papers fit radial velocities that we do not; per-night positions with unstated conventions; or a target the plan lists as not clean (HR 6819's Be-star disk).

items.title: awaiting fit
items.text: The fit, or the published reference, is not in yet. The tile shows whatever exists, such as the published orbit.

badges.pull: Each row of a table is one quantity, with virgil's value and its error beside the paper's. The pull is (virgil − paper) divided by the paper's quoted error on the side facing virgil. The pass limits were fixed before any fit was run: |pull| ≤ 0.25 for per-night positions and flux ratios, which come from the very same files and should nearly agree, and ≤ 2 for diameters and flux fractions. In the tables the pull is shaded by size: below 1σ, 1 to 3σ, above 3σ.
